paragraphs.text: This is an informal note by Chris Olah, published in 2023, about how neural networks pack information into their neurons. It looks at "distributed representations," a classic idea from neuroscience and AI where meaning spreads across many neurons instead of sitting in just one. The author argues this idea actually hides two different strategies, which he calls composition and superposition.

This matters because breaking a network's representations into separate, independent pieces is how researchers hope to actually understand what a network is doing. The two strategies behave very differently, so mixing them up leads to confusion about how networks generalize and what can be read out of them.

Composition means simple, independent features, like "color" and "shape," combine to build more complex ones. It uses fewer neurons, generalizes well to new combinations, and can be understood piece by piece. Superposition means packing more features than there are neurons, like squeezing many items into a small space; it needs a nonlinear step to retrieve them and can't easily be read out with a simple straight-line check.

The piece argues these two strategies compete for the same limited space, but sparsity, meaning features rarely all show up together, lets a network mix both at once. Telling composition and superposition apart matters, because only composition lets us understand a network using a small number of independent parts instead of an exploding mess of combinations.

fuller.text: This is an informal note, published in May 2023 by Chris Olah as part of the Transformer Circuits Thread, on how neural networks encode information. It examines "distributed representations," a long-standing idea from neuroscience and connectionist AI in which a concept is spread across many neurons rather than held by one. The note argues that this single label actually covers two distinct strategies, which it names composition and superposition.

This distinction matters because understanding the structure of a network's representations is central to reverse-engineering and mechanistically understanding neural networks. Splitting representations into independent components, rather than treating them as one tangled whole, is described as necessary for escaping the difficulties that come with very high-dimensional data.

Using examples of neurons representing colored shapes, the note contrasts a "local" code, one neuron per color-shape pair, with a "semi-local" compositional code, where separate color neurons and shape neurons combine. The compositional code needs far fewer neurons, lets learning about one combination transfer to others, and stays easy to interpret. A third, "dense" code uses superposition: it packs more feature combinations than it has neurons, gaining huge capacity but losing the ability to read out most features with a simple linear check, and losing the ability to represent in-between blends.

The note frames this as a genuine trade-off over a fixed "volume" of possible states. Features that fully compose can only fill a volume that grows linearly with the number of neurons, while superposition can store an exponentially larger number of items, but only if a nonlinearity is used to retrieve them. So the two strategies claim the same resource in incompatible ways.

Even so, the note shows the strategies can partly mix: when feature combinations are sparse, meaning many combinations rarely or never occur, the unused "holes" in a compositional code can be filled with other features held in superposition. The note concludes that distinguishing composition from superposition matters, since only composition lets a network's representation be understood as a manageable, linear number of independent parts.
